She needed no further encouragement.

"Well, my dear, Mrs. Long tells me that a wealthy young gentleman from the north of England has rented Netherfield. He drove down on Monday in a chaise drawn by four horses to inspect it, liked it so exceedingly that he made terms with Mr. Morris on the spot, and intends to move in before Michaelmas. Some of his servants will arrive by the close of next week."

"What is the gentleman called?"

"Bingley."

"Married, or unmarried?"

"Unmarried, my dear, naturally! A wealthy bachelor with four or five thousand a year. What a splendid opportunity for the girls!"

"In what way? What concern is it of theirs?"

"My dear Mr. Bennet," his wife answered, "why must you be so provoking? Surely you understand that I mean him to marry one of them."

"Is that his purpose in coming here?"

"Purpose! What nonsense you talk! But he may very well fall in love with one of them, and that makes it essential for you to call upon him as soon as he arrives."

"I can perceive no necessity. You and the girls can visit him, or send the girls alone, which might be wiser still. Since you are as handsome as any of them, Mr. Bingley may prefer you to the rest."

"You flatter me, my dear. I certainly have enjoyed my share of good looks, though I claim no unusual beauty now. A woman with five grown daughters ought to stop concerning herself with her own appearance."

"Such a woman seldom has much beauty left to concern herself with."

"Nevertheless, my dear, you really must visit Mr. Bingley once he settles in the neighbourhood."

"I assure you, that is more than I can promise."

"Think of your daughters! Imagine what a position such a marriage would give one of them. Sir William and Lady Lucas have resolved to call for that very reason, although, as you know, they ordinarily visit no newcomers. You absolutely must go, since we cannot possibly call unless you do."

"You are surely overparticular. I expect Mr. Bingley will welcome you gladly. I shall send a short note with you, giving my wholehearted consent to his marrying whichever daughter pleases him—though I must say something favourable about my little Lizzy."

"I insist that you do nothing of the kind. Lizzy is no better than her sisters. She is certainly not half as beautiful as Jane, nor half as cheerful as Lydia.

Our inspection continued until nightfall, when we left. On the homeward journey my companion briefly entered the offices of a daily newspaper.

I have mentioned my friend's many peculiar whims, and that Je les ménageais—a phrase without an English counterpart. His present inclination was to refuse any discussion of the murder until near midday on the following day. Then he abruptly asked whether I had noticed anything peculiar at the scene of the outrage.

The emphasis he placed upon "peculiar" made me shiver, though I could not have explained why.

"No, nothing peculiar," I answered. "At least, nothing beyond what we both read in the newspaper."

"The Gazette," he said, "has, I fear, failed to comprehend the extraordinary horror of the affair. But let us set aside that publication's empty opinions. To my mind, this mystery is thought impossible to solve for precisely the reason that ought to make its solution easy: the outre nature of its details. The police are bewildered by the apparent want of a motive, not for killing, but for the savagery of the killing. They also cannot reconcile the voices heard disputing with the discovery of nobody upstairs except the murdered Mademoiselle L'Espanaye, and with the absence of any exit through which someone might have escaped unnoticed by those ascending. The room's violent disorder, the body forced headfirst up the chimney, the old woman's frightfully mutilated remains—these facts, together with those already stated and others I need not enumerate, have brought the official investigators to a standstill by wholly defeating their vaunted acuteness. They have committed the serious but familiar mistake of treating the uncommon as necessarily obscure. Yet it is through departures from the ordinary that reason, if it advances at all, finds its path towards truth. In an inquiry like ours, the essential question is less 'What happened?' than 'What happened that has never happened before?' Indeed, the ease with which I shall reach—or have reached—the explanation stands in direct proportion to the impossibility the police perceive in the mystery."

I gazed at him in speechless amazement.

"At this moment I am expecting," he went on, glancing towards our apartment door, "a visitor who, while perhaps not himself responsible for these butcheries, must have had some degree of involvement in their commission.

Tom joined the newly formed Cadets of Temperance because he liked their flashy uniforms. He promised not to smoke, chew tobacco, or swear while he belonged to the group. Then he learned something new: promising not to do something is the surest way to make yourself want to do it. Before long he was tormented by the urge to drink and swear. It grew so strong that only the hope of showing off his red sash kept him from quitting. The Fourth of July was approaching, but he soon gave up waiting for that. Before he had spent forty-eight hours under these restrictions, he pinned his hopes on old Judge Frazer. The justice of the peace seemed to be dying, and such an important official would surely have a grand public funeral. For three days Tom followed the Judge's condition with intense interest, eagerly seeking news. Sometimes he became so hopeful that he took out his uniform and practised in front of the mirror. Unfortunately, the Judge had a discouraging habit of getting better and worse. Finally, people announced he was improving, then recovering. Tom was disgusted and felt personally wronged. He resigned immediately. That very night the Judge relapsed and died. Tom decided never to trust a man like that again.

The funeral was magnificent. The Cadets marched in a style that nearly killed their former member with envy. Still, Tom was free again, and that counted for something. Now he could drink and swear, but to his surprise he no longer wanted to. Knowing he was allowed to do those things took away both the desire and the attraction.

Soon Tom was surprised to discover that the holiday he had wanted so badly was beginning to feel rather dull.

He tried keeping a diary, but nothing happened for three days, so he gave it up.

The first minstrel show featuring caricatures of Black people came to town and caused a sensation. Tom and Joe Harper organized their own troupe of performers and enjoyed themselves for two days.

Even the Glorious Fourth was something of a disappointment. Heavy rain meant there was no parade. And Mr. Benton, a real United States Senator whom Tom considered the greatest man in the world, proved a terrible letdown. He was not twenty-five feet tall—not even remotely close to it.

Then a circus arrived.
